questionText:
Outline the winemaker's key considerations when deciding whether or not to filter each of the following in preparation for bottling:

a) white wine with 180g/L residual sugar
b) ruby port
c) Bourgogne Pinot Noir
commandWordDemand: In each case, candidates needed to consider how vulnerable the product is to post-bottling risks, requiring application of principles to each of the three styles of wine which had different levels of vulnerability.

coreRequirements.element: For each wine, consider whether not filtering is an option and why, i.e. how vulnerable the wine is to post-bottling risks such as in-bottle fermentation by yeast (S. cerevisiae or Brett) or malolactic bacteria

coreRequirements.temporalRationale: Structural or stable subject-matter demand; applies unchanged.

coreRequirements.element: Cover impact of filtration on quality, prior clarification, matching filtration type/pore size to wine style, microbial contamination risk, and re-fermentation risk
coreRequirements.quote: Areas to cover included: impact of filtration on wine quality; clarification before filtration to save time, filter wastage and money; understanding of the style of wine to determine the correct filtration process and then the type of filtration itself; filtration options and pore sizes; risks of microbial contamination; re-fermentation.
coreRequirements.temporalRationale: Structural or stable subject-matter demand; applies unchanged.

coreRequirements.element: (a) Recognise the 180g/L residual sugar wine as high risk of re-fermentation, requiring sterile filtration (0.45 micron), likely a late-harvest/botrytised wine needing glucanase enzymes and a filterability test
coreRequirements.quote: 180g/L residual sugar implies the risk of re-fermentation by yeast... The winemaker would always consider sterile filtration which is 0.45 micron.
coreRequirements.temporalRationale: Structural or stable subject-matter demand; applies unchanged.

coreRequirements.element: (b) Recognise Ruby Port is always filtered to avoid sediment (unlike a crusted style), using diatomaceous earth then a cellulose filter
coreRequirements.quote: LBV ports are always filtered to avoid sediment in a bottle (which would be acceptable in a crusted style).
coreRequirements.temporalRationale: Structural or stable subject-matter demand; applies unchanged.

coreRequirements.element: (c) Recognise Bourgogne Pinot Noir as typically dry, oak-aged and post-MLF, so relatively stable with little re-fermentation risk, making no filtration or only a light polishing filtration (~1.2 micron) an option
coreRequirements.quote: Candidates were expected to recognise that this may result in a relatively stable wine with little to no risk of re-fermentation going into bottle, so choosing not to filter is an option, or just a polishing filtration of around 1.2 microns.
coreRequirements.temporalRationale: Structural or stable subject-matter demand; applies unchanged.
